query: a bold, full-bodied red for a grilled steak dinner
answer:
For a grilled steak, here are my top three picks.

1. **Tenuta Sette Ponti 2005 Oreno, Toscana** (95 pts, $93) [2]. The reviewer pairs it specifically with "a rare steak cooked on a mesquite grill." It's a Sangiovese-Merlot-Cabernet blend with coffee, tobacco, leather and spice, and firm tannins that stand up to charred, fatty beef. It's the highest-scoring wine here and the one to open for a special occasion.

2. **Rocky Hill 2007 Richard Dinner Vineyards Red, Sonoma Mountain** (93 pts, $36) [5]. It's the best value of the six. This Malbec-Merlot-Syrah blend is bone dry with strong tannins, and its blackberry, cured meat and black pepper flavors suit a peppery crust. The review ends with "Grill up your best steak."

3. **Elvio Cogno 2011 Cascina Nuova Barolo** (93 pts, $58) [3]. It has a firm tannic backbone, with black cherry, licorice and a note of grilled herb. Its drinking window (2019–2031) puts it right in its prime now. Choose it if the guest likes savory, earthy reds more than plush fruit.

I left out a few of the others. The Fleming Jenkins Syrah [4] tastes like a perfect match, but the review gave it about five years before the fruit fades. A 2007 bottle is probably past that point by now. The Black Kite Pinot Noir [1] is described as big enough for steak, but Pinot is lighter than most guests expect when they ask for "bold and full-bodied." The PianCornello Brunello [6] also works, though the other three fit the request more closely.

My top pick's tasting note: Oreno [2] is a big Tuscan blend of coffee, tobacco, leather and spice with firm tannins and a long, spicy finish.

sources.title: Black Kite 2013 Redwood's Edge Pinot Noir (Anderson Valley)
Fleming Jenkins 2007 Madden Ranch Syrah (Livermore Valley)
Rocky Hill 2007 Richard Dinner Vineyards Red (Sonoma Mountain)

query: a crisp, mineral white to go with fresh oysters
answer:
For oysters you want high acidity, a dry finish and something saline or chalky. These three fit best.

**1. Hatzimichalis 2015 Assyrtiko, Atalanti Valley, Greece (91 pts, $12) [6]**
This is the most mineral wine in the set. The review notes a chalky backbone, compares it to Chablis (the classic oyster wine) and suggests oysters as a pairing. At $12 it is also the best value here.

**2. Kilikanoon 2014 Mort's Block Riesling, Clare Valley, Australia (92 pts, $20) [3]**
This is the crispest choice. It is very dry, with lemony citrus and a long, austere finish, and the review recommends it with oysters now. Pick this one if the guest wants lean and bracing more than chalky.

**3. Bodkin 2014 The Victor's Spoils Sauvignon Blanc, North Coast, California (91 pts, $18) [1]**
The review describes "almost electric acidity" with grapefruit, lime and herbs, and names raw oysters as a match. It is fruitier and more herbal than mineral, so it suits a guest who likes a zesty, aromatic style.

I left out the Grgich Hills [2] even though its review mentions oysters. Its rounded vanilla-cream layers make it richer than "crisp and mineral" suggests, and at $55 it is hard to justify here.

**Top pick in one line:** Hatzimichalis Assyrtiko [6]: chalky and Chablis-like, with a touch of spice and tropical fruit, for $12.

query: an elegant, silky Pinot Noir with red-berry fruit
answer:
For an elegant, silky Pinot built on red berries, these three fit best:

**1. Paul Cluver 2015 Cape Winemakers Guild Auction Selection Pinot Noir, Elgin (92 pts, price not listed) [1]**
The review calls it "silky and seductive" and "elegant and refined," so it matches your request most closely. Ripe red cherry and forest berries lead, with well-integrated tannins and enough acidity to keep it fresh. Cocoa, cola spice and forest floor add depth without weighing it down.

**2. Newton Johnson 2016 Cape Winemakers Guild Windansea Pinot Noir (92 pts, price not listed) [5]**
This one is also silky and smooth, with soft, fine tannins around red cherry and pressed flowers. It has more earth and sous bois than the others, a riper New World fruit core with an Old World, Burgundy-like savory side. Choose it if you like some forest floor alongside the fruit.

**3. Siduri 2010 Ewald Vineyard Pinot Noir, Russian River Valley (91 pts, $48) [4]**
If you want a California option with a known price, this is medium-bodied and silky, with ripe raspberry and cherry lifted by bright, citrusy acidity. It's made to drink well now, and it's still elegant enough for a good steak.

Baker Lane [3] is elegant too, but its fruit runs to tart cranberry and pomegranate, and the review doesn't call it silky. Thomas Fogarty [2] scores highest, but its review centers on a showy, fruit-punch aroma, so it fits a request for elegance less well.

My top pick, the Paul Cluver [1], has ripe red cherry and forest berry over a silky palate, with hints of cocoa and cola spice and a fresh finish of earthy baking spice.

query: an affordable Argentine Malbec under $20
answer:
Three of these come in under $20, and all three are well-reviewed Malbecs.

1. **Chaltén 2009 Gran Reserva Malbec (Neuquén)**: 92 pts, $19 [1]. This is the highest-scoring wine here under $20. It comes from Patagonian Neuquén, not Mendoza, and is full-bodied and layered, with blackberry, chocolate and coffee and a long, toasty finish that stays warm without turning hot.

2. **Proemio 2006 Reserve Malbec (Mendoza)**: 91 pts, $19 [3]. It's a good choice for a guest who likes some savory character: the nose has grilled steak, earthy berry and dry oak, and the palate is balanced, with blackberry, coconut, spice and textured tannins. Only 500 cases were made.

3. **Ricardo Santos 2006 La Madras Vineyard Malbec (Mendoza)**: 91 pts, $18 [2]. This is the cheapest of the three and the easiest to drink. It's ripe and bright, with cola, berry and herb aromas. The reviewer calls it "not overly complex," so it suits a casual bottle.

If $20 even fits the budget, Viña Cobos 2009 Felino [6] (91 pts) is a smooth, dense alternative. Trivento's Golden Reserve [5] goes just over the limit at $21.

These are all older vintages (2006–2009). The Chaltén review gives a drinking window "through 2017," and the Santos review says "the next year or two," so any bottle you find now may be past its best, or the shop may be selling a newer vintage that hasn't been reviewed.

**Top pick, Chaltén Gran Reserva [1]:** inky blackberry and graphite on the nose, with a deep palate of chocolate and coffee and a long, spicy, toasty finish.

sources.title: Ricardo Santos 2006 La Madras Vineyard Malbec (Mendoza)
Trivento 2010 Golden Reserve Malbec (Luján de Cuyo)

query: a dry Riesling from Germany with racy acidity
answer:
Here are three that fit: all dry, all German, and all built around high acidity.

**S.A. Prüm 2012 Graacher Dompropst GG Dry Riesling (Mosel), 94 pts, $75** [5]
This scores highest of the six. The reviewer calls it "racy," "dry in style," and "feather light," with grapefruit, green apple and lime over a steely, mineral edge. It is a Grosses Gewächs, the top dry category from a VDP estate, so it is worth the money for a special occasion.

**Staatliche Weinbaudomäne Oppenheim 2015 Niersteiner vom Rotliegenden Riesling (Rheinhessen), 91 pts, $28** [2]
If acidity is the main thing your guest wants, this is the most direct match. The note says "laser-edged," "dry and taut," and "spine tingling acidity," with concentrated lime and lemon and crushed-mineral tones. It costs well under half the price of the Prüm.

**Balthasar Ress 2015 Von Unserm Trocken Riesling (Rheingau), 91 pts, $22** [6]
This is the cheapest of the three. It is a lean, stony Rheingau trocken with green apple, fresh herbs and "racy streaks of lime and lemon," and it finishes with precision. It is a little slight in frame, so it suits a guest who likes their Riesling lean.

I left out the Johannishof Spätlese [1] because it is medium-dry rather than dry. The Berres [3] is technically dry, but its lush mango and guava character works against the lean style your guest asked for.

Top pick tasting note [5]: grapefruit, green apple and lime on a feather-light, steely palate, with a long, mouth-watering finish.

query: a rich, oaky California Chardonnay with buttery notes
answer:
Three bottles here fit a big, buttery, oak-driven California style well.

1. **Paul Hobbs 2010 Edwards James Estate Wente Selection Chardonnay, Russian River Valley** (95 pts, $75) [4]. The review calls it as rich and opulent as any Chardonnay out there, with smoky, buttered-toast and butterscotch oak over tropical fruit, honey and vanilla. Lime-driven acidity keeps all that weight from feeling heavy. It's the best match for your request and it's ready to drink now.

2. **Guarachi Family 2009 Chardonnay, Sonoma Coast** (92 pts, $30) [3]. It's described as "rich and oaky," with buttered toast, crème brûlée and vanilla over ripe pineapple jam. You get the big, powerful style for less than half the price of the Hobbs, and it's also ready now.

3. **Carte Blanche 2009 Chardonnay, Sonoma Coast** (93 pts, $75) [1]. Of these six, this one leans hardest on oak: buttered toast and butterscotch hit first, with pineapple and orange jam underneath. The reviewer found it "a bit jumbled" and suggested 3–4 years in the cellar, so it suits someone who plans to lay a bottle down more than someone opening it tonight.

On a tighter budget, the Kendall-Jackson Grand Reserve [6] ($21) is creamy, with vanilla and buttered-toast oak.

Top pick tasting note: Paul Hobbs [4] has tropical fruit, pear and honey wrapped in smoky butterscotch and buttered toast, with bright lime acidity on the finish.

Paul Hobbs 2010 Edwards James Estate Wente Selection Chardonnay (Russian River Valley)

query: a spicy, peppery Syrah from the Rhône
answer:
Only two of the six wines are actually Syrah from the Rhône, and both are from Cornas, where Syrah tends to be peppery and savory.

**1. Jean-Luc Colombo 2011 Terres Brulées, Cornas (94 pts, $48) [6]**
The review describes dried spices, cracked pepper and roasted meat that "scream of Syrah and the Northern Rhône," which is what the guest is asking for. It also has fine tannins and bright acidity, so it's easy to drink now and should keep through 2030. It's the highest score here and costs less than half as much as the next pick.

**2. Jean-Luc Colombo 2014 La Louvée, Cornas (93 pts, $104) [3]**
This one leads with peppery spice and anise over ripe blackberry-plum fruit, and its silky tannins keep the intensity in check. Choose it if the guest wants a more perfumed, plusher Cornas and doesn't mind the higher price.

**Outside the Rhône: Sequel 2007 Syrah, Columbia Valley (93 pts, $55) [4]**
This Syrah is from Washington, but the review says it "walks the line between the Rhône and Barossa," with pungent spice, meat and garrigue. It's bigger and oakier than the Cornas wines, so only offer it if the guest is open to a New World bottle.

**Top pick in one line:** Terres Brulées [6] has cracked pepper, dried spice and roasted meat over a medium-to-full body, with bright acidity and fine tannins.

sources.title: Bonny Doon 2013 Le Cigare Volant Red (Central Coast)

query: a smooth, easy-drinking red under $15 for a weeknight
answer:
None of these six wines is under $15. The cheapest is $19, so anything below means going about $4 or more over your budget. If you can stretch that far, these are the closest fits:

**Basilisco 2012 Teodosio, Aglianico del Vulture (92 pts, $19) [2]**
This one is the nearest to your price and the best match for what you described. The review calls it "remarkably easy drinking" and "a fantastic value," with a smooth palate and velvety tannins. It's full-bodied, but the juicy cherry and plum keep it friendly with pasta, pizza or a burger.

**Jaffurs 2014 Syrah, Santa Barbara County (91 pts, $29) [1]**
The review names it as a weeknight wine, with round blackberry and black currant fruit. It's more savory than the Basilisco, with notes of coffee, tar and slate, and at $29 it is about double your budget.

**Lecci e Brocchi 2012 Il Chiorba Riserva, Chianti Classico (91 pts, $36) [3]**
The review calls it "smooth, easy drinking and delicious," with polished tannins and fresh acidity, which makes it a good match for food. At $36 it is more of a weekend bottle, so it's here only if the style matters more to you than the price.

I'd skip [4], [5] and [6] for this request. They cost $40 to $70, and the Quinta de la Rosa [5] is tannic and isn't meant to be drunk until 2022.

**Top pick tasting note [2]:** Truffle, blackberry and dark chocolate on the nose, then a smooth palate of Marasca cherry, ripe plum and vanilla with velvety tannins.

query: a sparkling wine for a celebration
answer:
For a celebration, I'd pick these three:

**Schramsberg 2011 Méthode Traditionnelle Brut, Carneros** (93 pts, $75) [4]
This is the highest-scoring bottle here and a good one to open for a big moment. It's mostly Chardonnay with some Pinot Noir. Green apple, orange and grapefruit keep it bright, and biscotti-like creaminess fills it out, so it suits a toast and also works with food.

**Bellavista 2004 Gran Cuvée Brut Rosé, Franciacorta** (92 pts, price not listed) [1]
The reviewer suggests it for weddings and special outdoor occasions. It's a pale pink rosé with small-berry and bread-dough aromas and a firm, elegant finish, which makes it the most festive-looking glass of the group.

**Laetitia 2008 Brut de Blancs, Arroyo Grande Valley** (91 pts, $28) [2]
This is the one to buy if you're pouring for a crowd. The review calls it a good price for a wine this refined, with orange, lime, honey and toasty, yeasty notes. At $28 you can buy several bottles for less than one Schramsberg.

If the guest likes a richer, creamier style, Iron Horse's 2009 Russian Cuvée (92 pts, $38) [6] is a good alternative. It's mostly Pinot Noir and tastes of ripe apple and custard.

Top pick, Schramsberg [4]: a dry, doughy Carneros brut with green apple and grapefruit, biscotti creaminess and a long lemon-zest finish.

query: a sweet dessert wine to serve with a fruit tart
answer:
For a fruit tart, the wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert and have enough acidity to match the fruit. These three do that best:

1. **Castello di Bossi 2004 Vin San Laurentino, Toscana** (91 pts, $95) [2]. The review names fruit tarts as a pairing. Its dried apricot, orange and cinnamon flavors suit a pastry crust and baked or glazed fruit. It's the most expensive of the three, but it's the closest fit to what you asked for.

2. **Rosenhof 2012 Eiswein Blaufränkisch, Burgenland** (91 pts, $37) [3]. Use this one if the tart is built on tangy fruit like berries, red currants or passion fruit. Its sweetness and sharp acidity match those flavors, so the wine won't taste flat next to them. It's also an unusual bottle that guests will remember.

3. **Novy 2006 Oley Dessert Wine Viognier, Russian River Valley** (93 pts, $14) [6]. This is the best value and has the highest score of the group. It's very sweet and honeyed, with apricot and peach flavors that go well with stone-fruit or apricot tarts. It's quite rich, so pour small glasses.

I left out the Bonaccorsi Chardonnay [4] because it's bone dry, and dessert would make it taste thin and sour. The Sylvester Port-style Syrah [1] goes better with chocolate desserts than with fruit ones.

**Top pick tasting note:** amber in the glass, with maple syrup and dried orange on the nose, then dried apricot, hazelnut and cinnamon on a very smooth palate [2].

query: a age-worthy Bordeaux-style red blend for the cellar
answer:
Three of these suit a cellar especially well.

1. **Lauren Ashton Cellars 2009 Cuvée Arlette, Red Mountain (95 pts, $50) [5].** This is my top pick. It has the highest score of the six and the reviewer says it has "the power and tannin to age for decades." The blend leans on Merlot and Cabernet Franc, which puts it closer to a Right Bank Bordeaux than the Cabernet-heavy wines on this list. At $50 it costs a third as much as the California bottles.

2. **Captûre 2010 Harmonie, Pine Mountain-Cloverdale Peak (94 pts, $120) [3].** This is a high-elevation Cabernet-based blend from above Alexander Valley. The reviewer found hard tannins and concentrated cherry compote and cassis fruit, and suggested cellaring it for 8–10 years "if not longer." The note says the oak is in proportion to the fruit, which tends to bode well for long aging.

3. **Lineage 2009 Red Wine, Livermore Valley (94 pts, $145) [1].** This is a Cabernet-led blend that includes all five Bordeaux varieties. The reviewer calls it powerful yet focused, with leather, chocolate, dark plum and licorice, and advises laying it down "for a special occasion many years from now."

On timing: these reviews were written when the wines were young, and it is now 2026, so the 2009 and 2010 vintages are 16 to 17 years old. The "age for decades" claims for [5] and [3] give them the most room left. If you can find them, they should be drinking now and holding, and you won't be buying them to wait another ten years.

**Top pick tasting note:** Lauren Ashton Cuvée Arlette [5] is a tight, dark, dense Merlot-led blend, ripe and well proportioned, with enough tannin to age for decades.

query: a light, aromatic white with floral notes for a warm afternoon
answer:
For a warm afternoon, these three fit best:

1. **Aigner 2016 Ried Weinzierlberg Riesling (Kremstal)**: 91 pts, $16 [6]
   It has the most floral nose of the six, with jasmine and white blossom over tangerine and citrus. The body is very slender and the finish dry and brisk, so it stays refreshing in the heat. It's also the best value here.

2. **Salomon-Undhof 2013 Steinterrassen Riesling (Kremstal)**: 92 pts, $25 [1]
   This is the lightest and most thirst-quenching option. It's lemony, with a little spritz and a long, clean finish. The floral notes are only at the edges, so pick it if refreshment matters more to your guest than perfume.

3. **Dutton-Goldfield 2015 Dutton Ranch Shop Block Pinot Blanc (Green Valley)**: 92 pts, $30 [5]
   The reviewer calls it light, fresh and aromatic, with white peach, pear, floral grapefruit and a touch of ginger. It has a little more body than the two Rieslings while keeping lively acidity, which helps if the afternoon includes food.

I left out the Kracher [3] because it's a rich, sweet Trockenbeerenauslese, and the Waters blend [2] because it's described as palate-coating and rich. Both are lovely wines, just not light ones. The Knights Bridge [4] is floral, but its new-oak creaminess makes it heavier than the brief.

**Top pick tasting note [6]:** Jasmine and white blossom on the nose, then tangerine and clean citrus on a dry, brisk, very slender palate.

query: a Barolo with firm tannins and notes of tar and roses
answer:
Only one of these reviews mentions tar, roses and firm tannins together. The others each lack one of the three, so I've noted the gap for each.

1. **Rivetto 2008 Briccolina, Barolo (95 pts, $169) [2]**: This is the only one with all three. The nose has tar, dried roses and violets, and the review describes "tight tannins" with a polished texture. It has the highest score of the six, and it's the most expensive.

2. **Fontanafredda 2011 del Comune di Serralunga d'Alba (93 pts, $45) [4]**: The review gives rose and violet on the nose and "ripe, firm tannins" from Serralunga. It doesn't mention tar, but the licorice, tobacco and clove are in a similar dark, savory register. At $45 it's the best value if the guest cares more about structure than about tar specifically.

3. **Mauro Veglio 2006 Vigneto Gattera (91 pts, $45) [3]**: The nose has tar and pressed red rose, so the aromas are exactly right. The catch is the tannins: at about 20 years old they've softened to "smooth, silky," so it won't give the grip the guest asked for.

Top pick: Rivetto Briccolina 2008 [2], with tar, licorice and forest berry, dried violets and roses, and tight, polished tannins on a powerful palate.

query: a New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc with grapefruit and passion fruit
answer:
Your guest wants the classic Marlborough profile, and several of these wines name both fruits outright.

1. **Greywacke 2016 Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough** (91 pts, $23) [1]. Passion fruit leads on the nose, and white grapefruit builds on the plump palate. A light pea-tendril green note keeps it fresh, and the finish is long and citrusy. It is the closest match to what the guest asked for, made by Kevin Judd. If the 2016 is gone, the 2015 [2] at the same score and price has the same passion fruit and white grapefruit pairing with a silkier texture.

2. **Spy Valley 2014 Envoy Johnson Vineyard Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough** (93 pts, $33) [3]. It has the same passion fruit and grapefruit core, but the wine spent 11 months in oak, so it is dry and austere with smoky fumé and struck-match notes. Pick this if the guest wants a more serious, structured bottle and is fine spending $10 more.

3. **Te Mata 2013 Cape Crest Sauvignon Blanc, Hawke's Bay** (93 pts, $30) [4]. This is a riper style from outside Marlborough: passion fruit and pink grapefruit framed by vanilla and cedar from oak, with a creamy finish. It suits a guest who likes rounder whites more than zesty, green-edged ones.

Opawa [5] is good value at $15 and has plenty of passion fruit, but the review lists only "citrus," not grapefruit. Marisco [6] has grapefruit but no passion fruit. That is why I left both off the list.

Top pick tasting note: Greywacke 2016 has passion fruit and pea tendril on the nose, white grapefruit on a plump, medium-bodied palate, and a long, intense citrus finish.

query: an Oregon Pinot Noir under $40 with earthy forest-floor notes
answer:
None of these wines meets all three of your conditions. The Oregon bottles that have forest-floor notes cost more than $40, and the one Oregon bottle under $40 doesn't taste earthy. These three come closest.

**Adelsheim 2010 Pinot Noir, Willamette Valley (92 pts, $32) [2]**
This is the only Oregon Pinot here under your budget, and the review calls it "one of Oregon's best-value Pinot Noirs." Its flavors are tangy raspberry, dark chocolate and an espresso finish, so you'd get a racy, polished wine without the forest-floor note you asked for.

**Ross Andrew 2011 Reserve Lachini Vineyard Pinot Noir, Willamette Valley (92 pts, $50) [5]**
If the earthy character matters more to you than the price, this is the closest match. It's an Oregon wine whose aromas lead with forest floor, alongside strawberry and cola. It feels light on the palate but has plenty of flavor and a long finish. It costs $10 over your limit.

**Stephen & Walker 2006 Pinot Noir, Monterey (92 pts, $39) [1]**
If price and earthiness matter more to you than Oregon, this one has the forest-floor and mulch notes you described, at $39. It's from California and has a fuller, Burgundian style, with red and black cherry, licorice and cola over firm tannins.

My top pick is the Ross Andrew [5]: forest floor, strawberry and cola, light-bodied with a lingering finish.

query: a Napa Cabernet Sauvignon with cassis and cedar for a special occasion
answer:
For a special occasion, these three fit best:

1. **Caymus 2009 Special Selection Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley** (97 pts, $130) [1]. It's the highest-scoring wine on the list, and the reviewer names both cassis and "sweet, smoky cedar" among layers of blackberry tart, licorice and milk chocolate. It's big and ripe with soft tannins, the kind of bottle people remember from a celebration.

2. **Herencia 2013 Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley** (93 pts, $65) [3]. The review opens with cedar and cassis, so it matches the request closely. It's full-bodied but "restrained and elegant," which suits a guest who prefers polish to power. At half the Caymus price, it's also the best value of the three.

3. **Patel 2012 Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley** (92 pts, $110) [4]. Cassis and cedar lead here too, with black cherry and a firm, grippy structure. Pick this one if the guest likes a more structured, classic Cabernet over a lush one.

One caveat: all three are older vintages, and the drinking windows the reviewers gave end between 2020 and 2022. I'd buy them only from a source that can confirm good storage, and I'd expect more mature, savory flavors than the reviews describe.

Top pick, Caymus [1]: ripe blackberry, blueberry and cassis with smoky cedar, licorice and chocolate, soft tannins and a long finish.

sources.title: Caymus 2009 Special Selection Cabernet Sauvignon (Napa Valley)
Napa Cellars 2012 V Collection Cabernet Sauvignon (St. Helena)

query: a Champagne with brioche and toasty notes
answer:
For brioche and toast together, three of these stand out.

1. **Perrier Jouët 1998 Belle Epoque Brut** (94 pts, $150) [2]. The review names every note you asked for: toasty aromas, biscuit flavors and "pure brioche." The acidity is well integrated with the fruit, and at nearly a decade past vintage it is ready to drink now.

2. **Vincent Couche NV Extra Brut** (91 pts, $40) [1]. Toast and brioche are the first things on the nose, and for $40 it is the best value here. Long bottle age has replaced the youthful freshness with a mature, generous character. It is very dry but ripe, so serve it with food.

3. **Taittinger 2002 Comtes de Champagne Blanc de Blancs** (94 pts, $171) [4]. Bottle age gives it full, toasty depth, and a ripe, rounded mouthfeel sits on taut acidity. The review mentions no brioche, but the almond and citrus finish moves it in a nutty, savory direction. Pick this one if you prefer a finer, all-Chardonnay style.

**Top pick tasting note:** Perrier Jouët Belle Epoque 1998 [2] has toast and brioche on the nose, ripe fruit and biscuit on the palate, and well-integrated acidity.

query: a dry rosé from Provence for a summer lunch
answer:
For a summer lunch you want a rosé that is fresh and light on its feet, so these three suit it best:

1. **Château Roubine 2014 Premium Rosé**, Côtes de Provence (92 pts, $23) [2]. The reviewer calls it "a great summer rosé": crisp, with red currant and berry fruit, lively acidity and a tangy orange-peel finish. The review never actually says "dry," but nothing in the description suggests sweetness.

2. **Château la Mascaronne 2014 Quat'Saisons Rosé**, Côtes de Provence (91 pts, $23) [1]. The review names a light summer lunch as a good match. It is riper and rounder than the Roubine, with gentle fruit and enough acidity to stay fresh, so it would go well with grilled fish or a salade niçoise.

3. **Château Coussin 2010 Rosé**, Côtes de Provence Sainte-Victoire (92 pts, $20) [5]. This is the cheapest of the three and is explicitly described as dry. It is a textured, serious, food-friendly style, so it fits a lunch with real dishes on the table better than a glass on the terrace.

Watch the vintages. These reviews cover 2010 to 2014, and most Provence rosé is at its best within a year or two of bottling. Ask whether a current vintage of the same wine is available, because a bottle from those years may have lost its freshness.

I left out d'Esclans [4] and Muraires [6]. Both are fuller, richer food rosés, and at $35 and $59 they cost more than a light lunch needs.

**Top pick, Château Roubine [2]:** crisp red currants and berries, bright acidity and a tangy orange-peel finish.

query: a vintage Port with rich dark fruit and chocolate
answer:
Three bottles here fit a vintage Port with dark fruit and chocolate.

**Cockburn's 2009 Quinta dos Canais Vintage** (92 pts, $50) [1]
This is the closest match to what you asked for: ripe black plum and raisin with dark chocolate, plus a toffee-like smoothness. It also costs the least of the true vintage Ports on the list, and it's ready to enjoy now or over the medium term.

**Dow's 1963 Vintage** (95 pts, $467) [3]
After more than 40 years in bottle the tannins have softened, leaving a lush texture with rich fig and chocolate and a long finish with a touch of almond. It's a splurge for a special occasion. The review's drinking window ran to 2015, so it suits someone who likes very mature Port.

**Quinta do Vallado 2011 Vintage** (95 pts, $110) [2]
This one is dense and concentrated, with black plum, a sweet texture and dusty tannins from a strong vintage. The review doesn't mention chocolate, so pick it if you care more about dark fruit and structure.

The Occasio Opportunity Port [6] does show dark chocolate, but it's a non-vintage wine from California, not a vintage Port from the Douro, so I left it off the main list.

**Top pick, Cockburn's 2009 Quinta dos Canais [1]:** smooth and rich, with black plum, raisin, toffee, a hint of pepper and dark chocolate.

query: a Grüner Veltliner from Austria with white pepper
answer:
Every bottle on this list is an Austrian Grüner with white pepper in the tasting note. These three show it most clearly:

1. **Bernhard Ott 2014 Fass 4 Grüner Veltliner (Wagram)**, 92 pts, $32 [4]. Pepper runs from start to finish here. The nose has a peppery yeastiness, the slim citrus palate "reverberates constantly" with white pepper, and the finish tingles. If spice is what the guest wants most, this is the bottle.

2. **Geyerhof 2016 Rosensteig Grüner Veltliner (Kremstal)**, 94 pts, $20 [2]. This one is savory and intense: miso and peppery arugula on the nose, then lemon and a stony, salty finish edged with white pepper. It is the best value on the list, with the top score at the lowest price of the three.

3. **Bründlmayer 2013 Alte Reben Reserve Grüner Veltliner (Kamptal)**, 94 pts, $25 [5]. Old vines give it more weight and a creamy texture, with sage, arugula and white pepper at the core. Pour this for a guest who wants pepper in a rounder, more serious wine.

If the budget is tighter, the Wieninger 2015 Wiener Grüner Veltliner [3] costs $18 and shows a lighter dusting of pepper.

Top pick tasting note: Ott Fass 4 [4] is lean, zesty and citrus-led, with white pepper from nose to its tangy, tingling finish.

sources.title: Bründlmayer 2013 Alte Reben Reserve Grüner Veltliner (Kamptal)
